words.meaning: A system where society owns property and resources.

medium.simple_explanation: A political and economic system where property and resources are owned by the whole community rather than individuals.

examples.text: The rise of socialism in Europe challenged the idea that only the wealthy should hold power.

words.meaning: A sudden or major change in government or society.

medium.funny_explanation: Think of it as a total room makeover where you throw out everything you own and start from scratch overnight, but with more shouting and flags.

words.meaning: Having a lot of strength, influence, or control.

The state of being equal in status or rights.

The quality of being worthy of attention; importance.

Don't underestimate the significance of a single typo on a love letter.

words.meaning: Discussed the pros and cons of an issue.
Lands controlled by another country far away.

medium.funny_explanation: It's like when your big brother takes over your half of the bedroom and starts making rules about who can sit on your beanbag chair.

examples.text: Developments in the colonies helped shape new political ideas back in Europe.
The ants established several colonies in the kitchen after I dropped my jam toast.

words.meaning: Relating to society or the way people live together.

His societal contribution was inventing a machine that automatically dunks cookies in milk.

words.meaning: A complete change in the form or character.

hard.funny_explanation: A total makeover that makes the original thing completely unrecognizable—like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly.

examples.text: The industrial revolution led to a complete transformation of the economy.
After a bath and a haircut, the muddy stray dog underwent a magical transformation into a fluffy cloud.

hard.real_world_analogy: Like a 'before and after' home renovation where they tear down every wall to build a mansion.

words.meaning: Happening slowly or by small steps over time.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Used to describe the goal of those who wanted to organize society in a fundamentally different way.
hard.simple_explanation: To change the way something is organized or arranged.
hard.funny_explanation: Taking all the LEGO bricks apart and building something totally new because you didn't like the first castle.

examples.text: The new leaders wanted to restructure the government to give more power to the people.

hard.funny_explanation: Going from 'just a trim' at the barber to 'shave it all off' in one sitting.

examples.text: Liberals in the nineteenth century pushed for a nation that tolerated all religions.
The lunchroom liberals argued that every student should have the right to choose their own seat.

words.meaning: People who want deep and immediate social change.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: To identify the political group that wanted a government based on the majority and fast, extreme changes.

hard.funny_explanation: The 'all or nothing' squad who want to fire the principal and let the students run the school by Monday.

examples.text: The radicals wanted a nation where the government was based on the majority of the population.
My friends are radicals when it comes to spice; if it doesn't make them cry, it's not hot enough.

hard.real_world_analogy: Like a gamer who wants to delete the whole save file and start over because they made one tiny mistake.

words.meaning: The circumstances that form the setting for an event.

examples.text: We must understand what these political terms meant in the context of the nineteenth century.
Taking my text messages out of context makes me look like a crazy person who talks to cats.

hard.funny_explanation: The different flavors of chips in a 'Party Mix' bag; they are all chips, but they taste very different.

hard.real_world_analogy: Individual threads woven together to make a single piece of cloth.

examples.text: Liberals wanted a nation where various religious beliefs were tolerated.
My parents tolerated my drum practice for exactly ten minutes before the 'noise protest' started.

words.meaning: Treated someone unfairly based on their background.

hard.funny_explanation: Treating people differently just because of something they can't help, like hating everyone who wears blue socks.

words.meaning: To support or prefer one person or thing.
To disagree with or be against something.

medium.funny_explanation: Like a toddler with a permanent marker and a white wall—no limits, just pure chaos.

My dog’s uncontrolled excitement for treats results in him doing a backflip.

words.meaning: Related to a sequence of rulers from one family.

hard.funny_explanation: The ultimate family business where the 'promotion' is just waiting for your dad to retire (or worse) so you can wear the crown.

words.meaning: To protect something from being harmed or lost.

examples.text: They wanted to safeguard the rights of individuals against government overreach.

I am the official representative for the 'We Want More Recess' committee at home.

medium.funny_explanation: Like the universal law that the floor is lava the moment someone yells it.

examples.text: They did not believe in universal adult franchise, which is the right for every citizen to vote.
It is a universal truth that cats will sit in any cardboard box they find.

words.meaning: The legal right to vote in an election.

hard.funny_explanation: Not a fast-food chain, but the power to choose who runs the 'country-sized kitchen'.

hard.funny_explanation: Like a 'loading' screen when your internet is slow—it's going to happen, you just have to wait for it.

hard.real_world_analogy: The sunset. No matter how much you want it to stay light outside, the sun will definitely go down.

words.meaning: Relating to how a group of people live together.

medium.simple_explanation: Relating to society or how people live together in a community.
medium.funny_explanation: The silent rules that tell us it's okay to wear pajamas to bed but weird to wear them to a wedding.

hard.funny_explanation: A person who believes that your French fries are actually 'our' French fries.

examples.text: The communist manifesto argued for the end of private ownership.
In a communist kitchen, everyone cooks together and everyone shares the last cookie equally.

hard.real_world_analogy: A classroom where there are no private pencil boxes, and all stationery belongs to the whole class for everyone to use.

words.meaning: Completely sure about something.

words.meaning: Firmly requested or required something.

Convinced someone to do or believe something.

medium.simple_explanation: Convinced someone to do or believe something through reasoning or argument.
medium.funny_explanation: When you use logic, facts, and puppy-dog eyes to get your parents to extend your bedtime by 10 minutes.

examples.text: Lenin persuaded the committee to agree to his plan for a revolution.
I persuaded the cat that it was actually time for a bath, though the scratches on my arm say otherwise.

words.meaning: Taking something by force or sudden action.

medium.funny_explanation: The lightning-fast move you make to grab the TV remote before your brother can change the channel.

examples.text: The military committee planned a seizure of the government offices to gain power.
The sudden seizure of my fries by my best friend was a crime against snack-kind.

words.meaning: Formally chosen for a job or position.

medium.funny_explanation: Like being officially titled 'Chief Trash Taker-Outer' by your parents, but without the cool badge.

The dog was appointed the official guard of the front porch, but he mostly just slept.

words.meaning: Something kept hidden from others.
To call someone to come to a place.

medium.funny_explanation: When your mom yells your full middle name from the kitchen, you have been officially summoned and you better run!

examples.text: The Prime Minister left the city to summon loyal troops to fight the rebels.
I tried to summon my dragon during the history test, but unfortunately, it didn't show up.

words.meaning: Soldiers or armed forces.
The very first light of the day.
Remaining faithful to a person or government.
An answer or reaction to something.
To take someone into legal custody.
Fired heavy guns or explosives at a place.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: It refers to the ship Aurora firing heavy explosives at the Winter Palace to force a surrender.
hard.simple_explanation: Fired heavy explosives or large metal projectiles from big guns or ships.
hard.funny_explanation: Like throwing giant, explosive water balloons at a building, but much louder and way more destructive.

examples.text: The navy shelled the enemy fortifications from the coast to clear a path for the troops.
The squirrels shelled my garden with acorns until I finally went back inside.

hard.real_world_analogy: A heavy hailstorm hitting a tin roof, but the 'hail' is actually explosive cannonballs.

words.meaning: Large ships or boats.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Refers to the various ships that moved down the Neva river to seize military points during the revolution.
hard.simple_explanation: Large boats or ships used for transportation on water.
hard.funny_explanation: Giant floating bathtubs that carry people, cargo, or cannons instead of rubber ducks.

My paper boat is technically a vessel, even if it sinks the moment it hits a puddle.

hard.real_world_analogy: Just like a truck is a 'vessel' for cargo on a highway, a ship is a 'vessel' for cargo on the ocean.

words.meaning: The time when it becomes dark at night.
Stopped fighting and admitted defeat.

medium.simple_explanation: To stop fighting and admit that you have been defeated.
medium.funny_explanation: Waving a white sock in the air when your friends corner you during a water balloon fight.

examples.text: By the end of the night, the government ministers had surrendered to the Bolsheviks.
The army of ants finally surrendered after I moved my picnic blanket to the other side of the park.

words.meaning: Formally agreed to or accepted something.
Taking part in a physical struggle or battle.
To have power or command over something.
Belonging to the same or modern time.

hard.simple_explanation: Belonging to the same time period or the present time.
hard.funny_explanation: Listening to the latest pop hits instead of the music your great-grandparents danced to.

examples.text: Contemporary artists often use digital tools that weren't available fifty years ago.
My fashion sense is contemporary, which is a fancy way of saying I just wear whatever is clean today.

hard.real_world_analogy: A live news broadcast showing what is happening right now, compared to a history documentary.

words.meaning: A system to organize days, months, and years.
The act of giving up a position of power.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: It marks the moment Tsar Nicholas II officially gave up his throne and ended the monarchy in Russia.
hard.simple_explanation: The formal act of giving up a high office, position, or authority.
hard.funny_explanation: The ultimate 'I quit!' move, but specifically for kings and queens.

examples.text: The king's abdication led to a period of political uncertainty in the country.
After seeing the mountain of dishes, I announced my abdication as the Chief Kitchen Cleaner.

hard.real_world_analogy: Handing over the TV remote to someone else because you're tired of picking the channel.

words.meaning: Relating to the people within a country.

medium.simple_explanation: Relating to ordinary citizens or their concerns, rather than military or religious matters.
medium.funny_explanation: A 'civil' war is a very ironic name, because fighting with your neighbors is usually not very polite or 'civil' at all!

examples.text: After the revolution, the country fell into a civil war between different groups of citizens.
There was a civil war in my house over whether pineapple belongs on pizza.

words.meaning: Bringing small farms together into one large group.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Refers to the later Soviet policy of merging individual farms into large, state-controlled units.
hard.simple_explanation: Organizing something, like farms, into groups that are owned and managed by the state or a group.
hard.funny_explanation: Imagine if you and all your neighbors had to throw your lunch boxes into one big bucket and then everyone shared the contents.

examples.text: The government introduced collectivisation to increase agricultural production through shared resources.
The 'collectivisation' of my pens at school means I never have one when I actually need it.

hard.real_world_analogy: Turning several small family gardens into one giant community park where everyone works and shares the vegetables.

words.meaning: Member of the majority faction of the Russian party.

medium.simple_explanation: A member of the radical political group that seized power during the Russian Revolution.
medium.funny_explanation: The ultimate party-crashers who ended up owning the entire house.

examples.text: The Bolsheviks renamed themselves the Russian Communist Party after taking power.
If a Bolshevik organized a school dance, they would probably decide everyone has to wear the same color and dance the same way.

words.meaning: Given a new or different name.
Process of voting to choose a representative.
Having the power to create a constitution.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The Bolsheviks held elections for the Constituent Assembly, which was supposed to draft the new rules for Russia.
hard.simple_explanation: A group of representatives who are given the power to create or change a country's constitution.
hard.funny_explanation: Imagine a group of students chosen specifically to rewrite the school's 'No Homework' policy into a law.

examples.text: The Constituent Assembly was dismissed by Lenin because it did not support his party's views.
The dog's constituent assembly voted 10-0 that 'fetch' is now an optional activity.

hard.real_world_analogy: Like a committee formed to write the fundamental rules of a new gaming club.

words.meaning: A group of people gathered for a purpose.

medium.simple_explanation: A large group of people who meet to make laws or decisions for a country.
medium.funny_explanation: Like a giant school meeting where everyone tries to talk at once, but with more fancy suits and higher stakes.

examples.text: The Constituent Assembly was elected to decide on Russia's new government.
The student assembly voted for free pizza, but the principal dismissed them just like Lenin did.

words.meaning: More than half of the total number.
Refused to accept or agree to something.
Actions taken to achieve a specific result.

medium.simple_explanation: Official actions or laws taken by a government to deal with a situation.
medium.funny_explanation: Not the kind of 'measure' where you use a ruler, but the kind where the government says, 'Here is how things are going to be!'

words.meaning: Sent away or removed from a position.

medium.simple_explanation: To officially tell a group or person that their services are no longer needed or that they must leave.
medium.funny_explanation: The political version of saying 'You're fired' and 'Go home' at the same time.

examples.text: Lenin dismissed the Assembly after it refused to follow his lead.
I dismissed the idea of doing homework once I saw that my favorite movie was on TV.

words.meaning: Based on the principle of equal rights.
Not sure or not clearly known.
Strong disagreement with a person or plan.

medium.simple_explanation: A person or group who disagrees with the main group in power.
medium.funny_explanation: The people who are professional 'no-sayers' to whatever the leaders want to do.

examples.text: The Bolsheviks made peace with Germany despite strong opposition from other parties.
My cat is the main opposition to my plan of having a clean, fur-free sofa.

words.meaning: Groups that cooperate with each other.

medium.simple_explanation: Groups or countries that work together for a common purpose.
medium.funny_explanation: The friends you team up with in a game, right until someone wants to hog all the loot.

examples.text: Even their political allies were surprised when the Bolsheviks signed the peace treaty.
The squirrels and the pigeons were allies in the Great Park Breadcrumb War.

words.meaning: To take part in an activity.
Group of people who make laws.
Made to suffer for a mistake.
Expressed disapproval of someone or something.

medium.simple_explanation: Expressed disapproval or pointed out the faults in something.
medium.funny_explanation: Giving a thumbs-down to someone's work, but sometimes it gets you in big trouble with the secret police.

examples.text: The secret police punished anyone who criticised the Bolshevik government.
I criticised the dog for eating my homework, but he just wagged his tail like it was a compliment.

words.meaning: Came together for a common cause.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The text mentions that young writers and artists rallied to the Bolshevik Party because they wanted change.
hard.simple_explanation: To come together and unite in support of a specific cause or person.
hard.funny_explanation: When your friend opens a bag of chips and everyone suddenly 'unites' around them within three seconds.

examples.text: Supporters rallied to the leader after the powerful speech.
The neighborhood cats rallied to the backyard when they heard the sound of the tuna can opening.

hard.real_world_analogy: Like a sports team huddling together before a big match to boost their spirit.

words.meaning: Economic system where society owns property.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Young people supported the Bolsheviks because the party stood for the principle of socialism.
hard.simple_explanation: A political and economic system where property and resources are owned or controlled by the community or government.
hard.funny_explanation: A system where if you have two cookies, the government asks you to share one with your friend who has zero.

examples.text: Socialism aims to reduce the gap between the rich and the poor through common ownership.
In my version of kitchen socialism, everyone shares the chores, but somehow I'm the only one doing the dishes.

hard.real_world_analogy: A potluck dinner where everyone brings a dish to share with everyone else instead of eating alone.

words.meaning: Losing belief in someone or something.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Artists became disillusioned because the Bolshevik Party began controlling what they could create.
hard.simple_explanation: Losing your belief or trust in something after discovering it is not as good as you expected.
hard.funny_explanation: That feeling when you realize the 'Giant Chocolate' box is 90% air and only 10% chocolate.

examples.text: The voters felt disillusioned when the politician failed to keep his promises.
I was disillusioned with the magic show when I saw the rabbit hiding in the magician's sleeve.

hard.real_world_analogy: Ordering a gourmet burger from a picture and receiving a squashed bun with a sad pickle.

words.meaning: Limiting information or ideas in the media.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The Bolshevik Party encouraged censorship, leading to dissatisfaction among creative people.
hard.simple_explanation: The suppression or prohibition of parts of books, films, or news that are considered politically unacceptable or 'harmful'.
hard.funny_explanation: When your parents 'beep' out the bad words in your favorite songs so you don't repeat them.

examples.text: Censorship prevents people from expressing their true opinions about the government.
The dog practiced strict censorship by barking loudly every time my cat tried to meow.

hard.real_world_analogy: A bouncer at a club who only lets 'approved' words and ideas into the conversation.

words.meaning: Public meeting to show an opinion.

medium.simple_explanation: A public meeting or march to show feelings about a political issue.
medium.funny_explanation: A giant group walk where you get to hold signs and yell about things you want to change.

examples.text: A massive May Day demonstration took place in Moscow in 1918.
The toddlers organized a demonstration to demand more snacks and fewer naps.

words.meaning: To be against someone or something.
Things that are owned by someone.
Placed under the control of the government.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The Bolsheviks nationalised industries and banks, taking them away from private owners.
hard.simple_explanation: When the government takes control and ownership of a private business or industry.
hard.funny_explanation: Imagine if the principal 'nationalised' your lunch box and decided everyone gets exactly three carrots and half a sandwich.

examples.text: The government nationalised the coal mines to ensure better working conditions.
I nationalised the TV remote so that the family would stop fighting over which channel to watch.

hard.real_world_analogy: Turning a private road that charges a toll into a public highway owned by the city.

words.meaning: Process of dealing with or controlling things.
To take hold of something forcibly.

medium.simple_explanation: To take hold of something suddenly and by force.
medium.funny_explanation: The political version of 'finders keepers,' except the people you're taking it from are definitely not happy.

examples.text: Peasants were encouraged to seize the land owned by the nobility.
I had to seize the TV remote before my sister could put on her boring documentaries.

words.meaning: People belonging to a high social class.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Peasants were allowed to seize the land of the nobility, who were the wealthy upper-class landowners.
hard.simple_explanation: A group of people belonging to the highest social class, usually with hereditary titles like Duke or Count.
hard.funny_explanation: People who think they are better than you because their great-great-grandfather once owned a very fancy horse.

examples.text: In old Russia, the nobility owned most of the land while the peasants did all the work.
My cat acts like she belongs to the nobility, demanding her food be served on a silver plate.

hard.real_world_analogy: The VIP lounge at an airport where only certain 'important' people are allowed to sit.

words.meaning: Made sure a rule was followed.

medium.simple_explanation: Made sure that people obeyed a rule or law.
medium.funny_explanation: When a leader stops asking nicely and starts making sure you actually do what you're told.

examples.text: The Bolsheviks enforced the division of large houses to accommodate more families.
The 'no phones at the table' rule was strictly enforced by my grandma with a wooden spoon.

words.meaning: Dividing something into two or more parts.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The Bolsheviks enforced the partition of large houses to fit multiple families based on their needs.
hard.simple_explanation: The act of dividing something into smaller parts or sections.
hard.funny_explanation: That invisible line you draw on the car seat to make sure your sibling doesn't breathe on your side.

examples.text: The partition of the large hall created three separate meeting rooms.
The partition of the pizza was unfair; my brother got the half with all the pepperoni.

hard.real_world_analogy: Putting a curtain across a room to turn it into two separate bedrooms.

words.meaning: Things that are needed or wanted.
To officially stop something from happening.
Supporting a sudden, complete change in government.

medium.simple_explanation: Wanting to completely change the way a country or system works, often through force.
medium.funny_explanation: It's like deciding to replace all your textbooks with video games overnight—a total, massive change!

examples.text: The revolutionary group wanted to overthrow the king and start a new government.
I have a revolutionary plan to make school lunches consist entirely of ice cream.

words.meaning: A rebellion or revolt against those in power.

medium.simple_explanation: An act of resistance or rebellion; a group of people standing up against those in power.
medium.funny_explanation: Imagine the whole school suddenly refusing to do homework at the same time—that's a student uprising!

examples.text: The peasants organized an uprising to protest the unfair taxes.
The cats in the neighborhood started an uprising against the local dog park.

words.meaning: A feeling of strong excitement or interest.
A large country house on a big estate.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Describes the large country houses of the Russian elite that were targeted and looted during the 1917 revolution.
hard.simple_explanation: A large country house with lands, usually belonging to a wealthy landowner.
hard.funny_explanation: A house so massive it has its own zip code and enough rooms for you to get lost and not be found for three days.

examples.text: The angry peasants marched toward the manor to demand land redistribution.
Living in a manor sounds cool until you realize it takes forty minutes to walk to the kitchen for a snack.

hard.real_world_analogy: Like a 'boss level' estate in a video game that comes with its own forest and servants.

words.meaning: Stole property by force, usually during a war.

medium.simple_explanation: Stole things from a place, usually during a war, riot, or period of chaos.
medium.funny_explanation: Like a pirate raid, but without the cool eyepatches and parrots.

examples.text: During the confusion of the battle, the city shops were looted.
My little brother looted my secret candy stash while I was at practice.

words.meaning: Formally taken by an authority for military use.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Refers to the act of the revolutionary government or peasants taking over private farms and property for public use.
hard.simple_explanation: When the government or an authority officially takes something for public or military use.
hard.funny_explanation: When your mom takes your phone 'for your own good'—it's not stealing, it's a requisition.

examples.text: The state requisitioned all the wheat to feed the hungry city dwellers.
My older brother requisitioned my laptop because he said his school project was more 'historically significant' than my gaming.

hard.real_world_analogy: Like a teacher confiscating a fidget spinner because it's 'disrupting the collective peace' of the classroom.

words.meaning: Extremely big in size, area, or amount.
Gave out shares of something to several people.

medium.simple_explanation: Gave out or shared portions of something among a group of people.
medium.funny_explanation: Think of a card dealer passing out cards, but instead of cards, it's land (and hopefully nobody cheats).

examples.text: The teacher distributed the graded tests to the students.
I distributed the pizza slices very carefully, making sure I got the biggest one.

words.meaning: Relating to a council or the Russian government.

medium.simple_explanation: An elected council of workers or peasants in the former Russian empire.
medium.funny_explanation: It's like a school council, but instead of planning dances, they were trying to run a whole country.

examples.text: The local Soviet met to decide how to manage the village's food supply.
If our cafeteria had a Soviet, we'd probably vote for extra dessert every day.

words.meaning: A large piece of land owned by a person.

medium.simple_explanation: A large piece of land in the country, usually with a big house, owned by one person or family.
medium.funny_explanation: A yard so big you might need a map and a packed lunch just to walk to the front gate.

examples.text: The wealthy family lived on a beautiful estate with many gardens.

words.meaning: A sudden and illegal take-over of power.

hard.simple_explanation: A sudden, violent, or illegal takeover of a government.
hard.funny_explanation: When the toddlers in the nursery decide they are done with naps and lock the teachers in the supply closet.

examples.text: The military coup replaced the old president with a new general overnight.

hard.real_world_analogy: A hostile takeover in a business where a new CEO walks in and tells the old boss to pack their bags immediately.

words.meaning: Too difficult, painful, or annoying to handle.

hard.simple_explanation: To guarantee that something is true or that someone is reliable.
hard.funny_explanation: When your friend tells your parents 'he was with me the whole time' to cover for your late arrival.

examples.text: The chairman said he would vouch for the safety of the family during the riots.

hard.real_world_analogy: A five-star rating on an app where you tell others, 'Trust me, this actually works.'

words.meaning: Something that is owned by a person.
Stories or news that might not be true.
To legally force someone to leave a building.

hard.simple_explanation: To legally or forcefully remove someone from a property.
hard.funny_explanation: What happens to a spider when you find it in the bathtub and use a cup to 'move' it outside.

hard.real_world_analogy: Getting kicked out of a movie theater for talking too loudly; you are being 'evicted' from your seat.

words.meaning: Groups of people chosen to make decisions.

medium.simple_explanation: Groups of people chosen to do a specific job or make decisions.
medium.funny_explanation: Groups of people who meet to discuss why they need to have another meeting.

examples.text: The village formed several committees to organize the new school.
My family has various committees, mostly for deciding what to watch on TV.

words.meaning: To feel or show great joy or happiness.

medium.simple_explanation: To feel or show great joy or happiness.
medium.funny_explanation: That feeling when you find out your dentist appointment was canceled and you get to stay home instead.

examples.text: The people began to rejoice when they heard the war was finally over.
I shall rejoice when the Wi-Fi finally starts working again!

words.meaning: An inner sense of what is right or wrong.

hard.simple_explanation: The inner sense of what is right or wrong in one's conduct.
hard.funny_explanation: That annoying little voice in your head that tells you 'no' right when you're about to do something fun but stupid.

examples.text: Her conscience wouldn't let her keep the money she found on the street.
My conscience is very clear, mostly because I don't use it very often.

hard.real_world_analogy: A built-in moral GPS that starts 'recalculating' and beeping when you take a wrong turn in life.

words.meaning: Done in a kind and sympathetic way.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Refers to the kind or compassionate treatment of the estate owners by the revolutionary peasants.
hard.simple_explanation: In a way that shows compassion, kindness, or respect for human life.
hard.funny_explanation: Trying to catch a mosquito with a cup to let it outside instead of just squishing it.

examples.text: The prisoners were treated humanely and provided with food and medicine.

hard.real_world_analogy: Giving a competitor a high-five after they lose the game instead of laughing at them.

words.meaning: Sharing something out in a new or different way.

medium.simple_explanation: The act of giving something out again in a different way, often to make it fairer.
medium.funny_explanation: Taking all the extra snacks from the kid who has twenty and giving some to the kids who have zero.

examples.text: The redistribution of land allowed many poor farmers to own their own fields.
The redistribution of chores meant that my older brother finally had to wash the dishes.

words.meaning: Left the army without permission.

medium.simple_explanation: Left a place or person without permission, especially leaving the army.
medium.funny_explanation: Leaving your post so fast that there’s a human-shaped hole in the wall.

words.meaning: People open to new ideas and individual freedoms.

hard.funny_explanation: A household where the cat decides when everyone wakes up, what everyone eats, and who is allowed to use the laptop.

examples.text: The Russian revolution aimed to end the autocracy of the Tsar.
Group projects often turn into an autocracy when one person decides they are the only smart one.

hard.real_world_analogy: A classroom where there are no votes, no debates, and the teacher makes every single rule without asking anyone.

words.meaning: A group of states or territories under one ruler.
An increase in size, number, or importance.
An extreme shortage of food in a region.

medium.simple_explanation: An extreme shortage of food that causes many people to go hungry.
medium.funny_explanation: It's like when you're 'starving' because lunch is ten minutes late, but way more serious and scary.

examples.text: Russian colonists moved into Central Asia and often clashed with the local people.

medium.simple_explanation: Brutally killed a large number of people at once.

hard.real_world_analogy: Applying a healing ointment to a scratch so it stops hurting.

words.meaning: Relating to the government of a country
The right of a country to govern itself

medium.simple_explanation: The right or power of a group to govern themselves and make their own decisions.
medium.funny_explanation: Autonomy is finally being old enough to choose your own haircut without your parents crying about it.

examples.text: Many regions in the Soviet Union were promised autonomy so they could manage their own local affairs.
The cat has complete autonomy in this house; she sleeps wherever she wants and we just deal with it.

words.meaning: Rules or plans made by a government
Living by moving from place to place

medium.simple_explanation: A way of life where people do not live in one place but move around to find food or work.
medium.funny_explanation: It is like being on a permanent camping trip where your house moves as often as your socks do.

examples.text: The government tried to stop nomadism and forced people to settle in permanent villages.
My brother's lifestyle is basically nomadism; he wanders from the sofa to the fridge and back again all day.

words.meaning: Achieving a desired aim or result
A big change in how a country is governed
Someone who wants to change the government completely

medium.simple_explanation: Someone who wants to completely change the government or the way society works.
medium.funny_explanation: A person who decides that spoons are better than forks for eating steak is a kitchen revolutionary.

examples.text: M.N. Roy was a famous Indian revolutionary who worked to change the political systems in many countries.
The student who suggested a four-day school week was treated like a hero and a revolutionary.

words.meaning: Important and well-known

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: M.N. Roy is described as a prominent leader in the communist movement.
hard.simple_explanation: Important, famous, or very easy to notice.
hard.funny_explanation: Being the person in the group photo who accidentally wore a neon green shirt while everyone else wore black.

examples.text: He played a prominent role in the fight for independence.
The giant pimple on my nose was unfortunately very prominent during the school photo.

hard.real_world_analogy: A skyscraper in a town full of small huts.

words.meaning: A person who leads or commands a group
Kind and helpful

medium.simple_explanation: Well-meaning, kind, and generous.
medium.funny_explanation: Think of a benevolent billionaire who buys everyone in the world a free taco just because it's Tuesday.

examples.text: The chieftain was a benevolent man who took care of the people in his tribe.
I am a benevolent ruler of my room; I allow the spiders to live in the corner as long as they don't pay rent.

words.meaning: A young person
Removed from power by force

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The text refers to the revolution that overthrew the Tsar.
hard.simple_explanation: To remove a leader or government from power by force.
hard.funny_explanation: The ultimate 'you're fired' but delivered by an entire angry population.

examples.text: The corrupt dictator was finally overthrown by a popular uprising.
The cat's reign of terror on the kitchen counter was overthrown when the dog learned to jump.

hard.real_world_analogy: Knocking over a king piece in a game of chess.

words.meaning: People who have control over something
A feeling of anxiety or dismay

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The Kirghiz people reacted to the violent October Revolution with consternation.
hard.simple_explanation: A feeling of shock, worry, or confusion caused by something unexpected.
hard.funny_explanation: The face you make when you see the 'Total Amount Due' on your credit card bill after a vacation.

examples.text: To the consternation of the students, the teacher announced a surprise test.
There was great consternation when the ice cream truck drove past our house without stopping.

hard.real_world_analogy: The feeling in a crowded room when the lights suddenly go out and someone screams.

words.meaning: Cruel or unfair treatment of people

medium.simple_explanation: Cruel or unfair treatment of a person or group by those in power.
medium.funny_explanation: The feeling of deep oppression when your teacher assigns a 10-page essay on a Friday afternoon.

examples.text: The people hoped the revolution would end the long years of oppression under the Tsar.
My dog thinks that not getting a second dinner is a form of systematic oppression.

words.meaning: A feeling of wanting something to happen
Fully achieved or made real

medium.simple_explanation: To make something that was just a dream or a plan actually happen.
medium.funny_explanation: When you finally 'realised' your plan to build a fort out of every pillow in the house.

examples.text: The people hoped that their dream of having their own government would finally be realised.
I realised my goal of sleeping for twelve hours, but then I realized I missed breakfast.

words.meaning: Stealing things using violence during war

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The second revolution was accompanied by violence and pillage.
hard.simple_explanation: The act of stealing things using force, especially during a war or riot.
hard.funny_explanation: Basically extreme, non-consensual shopping with zero intention of paying.

examples.text: The invading army began to pillage the small villages along the border.
I went to pillage the fridge at midnight, but all I found was half a lemon and some old yogurt.

hard.real_world_analogy: A pirate crew raiding a treasure island.

words.meaning: Having total power over a country

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The text describes the establishment of dictatorial power following the revolution.
hard.simple_explanation: Having total control and forcing people to obey without listening to their opinions.
hard.funny_explanation: That one friend who decides where everyone eats, what movie they watch, and what time they breathe.

examples.text: The new leader ruled with dictatorial authority, banning all opposition.
My toddler's dictatorial demands for 'more juice' must be met immediately or there will be a tantrum.

hard.real_world_analogy: A classroom where the teacher never lets anyone ask questions or use the bathroom.

words.meaning: The ability or right to control people
Officials who work in a government department

medium.simple_explanation: Government officials who work in large offices and are often associated with complicated rules and paperwork.
medium.funny_explanation: These are the people who make you fill out a form to get a form that allows you to buy a stamp.

examples.text: Even after the revolution, many of the same bureaucrats remained in their office jobs.
If bureaucrats ran a lemonade stand, you would need a permit, a safety inspection, and three signatures just for one cup.

words.meaning: To make something continue for a long time

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The Kazakh leader noted that the new government was continuing to perpetuate the same oppressive regime as before.
hard.simple_explanation: To make a situation or a system continue for a long time.
hard.funny_explanation: Keeping a bad habit alive even when everyone knows it’s a terrible idea.

examples.text: Spreading rumors only serves to perpetuate the conflict.
Why do you perpetuate the lie that you actually enjoy eating kale?

hard.real_world_analogy: Keeping a campfire going by adding more logs so it never burns out.

words.meaning: A system of government, often an unfair one

medium.simple_explanation: A particular government or a system of doing things, especially one that is very strict.
medium.funny_explanation: My gym teacher has a 'no-talking' regime that makes the locker room feel like a top-secret submarine.

examples.text: The new regime promised freedom but ended up being just as strict as the old one.
Under the new snack regime in my house, cookies are only allowed on days that end in 'y'.

words.meaning: A group of people living and working together.

medium.simple_explanation: A group of people living together and sharing possessions and responsibilities.
medium.funny_explanation: Imagine a giant sleepover that never ends, where you have to share your snacks and your chores with everyone.

examples.text: The workers moved into a commune to share the costs of living and farming.
Living in a commune sounds great until you realize you have to share your favorite hoodie with thirteen other people.

words.meaning: Shared by all members of a community.
Basic rules or beliefs that guide actions.

medium.simple_explanation: The basic rules or beliefs that guide how a person or group behaves.
medium.funny_explanation: Basically the 'moral compass' that keeps you from eating the last slice of pizza without asking.

examples.text: The society was founded on the principles of equality and shared labor.
My personal principles strictly forbid me from doing homework before I've had at least one snack.

words.meaning: Working together to reach a common goal.
Money or profit gained from an activity.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Describes how the total earnings or results of the members' hard work were shared among everyone in the commune.
hard.simple_explanation: The total amount of money or profits earned from a particular activity or sale.
hard.funny_explanation: The 'loot' you get after a long day of work, which in a commune, gets split up before you can even hide it under your mattress.

examples.text: The proceeds from the village fair were donated to the local hospital.
The proceeds from my lemonade stand were exactly five rupees and a half-eaten biscuit.

hard.real_world_analogy: The massive pile of candy a group of friends collects on Halloween and then dumps on the floor to divide equally.

words.meaning: Places where people live, such as houses.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Refers to the houses or living quarters that were shared by the members of the Soviet collective farms.
hard.simple_explanation: Places where people live, such as houses, apartments, or shelters.
hard.funny_explanation: The fancy word for 'the box where you keep your bed and your snacks.'

examples.text: The government built new dwellings for the workers near the industrial site.
My cat believes that all cardboard boxes in this house are his personal dwellings.

hard.real_world_analogy: A bird's nest or a beehive—it's the specific spot where an inhabitant rests and stays safe.

words.meaning: Places or equipment provided for a purpose.
Brought under the control of the government.

medium.simple_explanation: When the government takes control of a private industry or business.
medium.funny_explanation: It's like if the principal suddenly decided they owned all the snack machines in the school and decided who gets the chips.

examples.text: The Bolsheviks nationalised the banks to gain control over the nation's money.
If my mom nationalised my bedroom, she'd probably turn it into a laundry folding station.

words.meaning: Allowed something to happen or be done.
Small farmers or people who work on land.
Taken away by an authority as a penalty.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Refers to land and property taken away from private owners (like the nobility or wealthy peasants) by the Bolshevik government.
hard.simple_explanation: Taken away by an authority figure, usually as a punishment or for public use.
hard.funny_explanation: The tragic moment when a teacher grabs your phone because you were texting under the desk.

examples.text: The customs officer confiscated the illegal goods at the airport.
Mom confiscated my video game console until I finished my math homework.

hard.real_world_analogy: A referee taking the ball away from a player who keeps breaking the rules.

words.meaning: Done by people acting as a group.

medium.simple_explanation: Done by people acting as a group rather than individuals.
medium.funny_explanation: Like a group project where everyone actually does their part and you all get the same (hopefully good) grade.

examples.text: The government encouraged collective farming to increase the food supply.
Our collective effort to find the TV remote involved moving every cushion in the house.

words.meaning: Controlled by a single main authority.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Describes the Soviet economic system where all decisions and planning were made by a single central authority in the government.
hard.simple_explanation: Controlled by a single, main authority or located in one central place.
hard.funny_explanation: Like a household where one person holds the TV remote and decides what everyone else has to watch.

examples.text: The company moved to a centralised system to manage all its branches from one office.
Our kitchen is a centralised snack station for every kid in the neighborhood.

hard.real_world_analogy: An octopus using one brain to tell all eight arms exactly what to do at the same time.

words.meaning: Carefully judged the value or quality of something.

medium.simple_explanation: To carefully judge or evaluate a situation or value.
medium.funny_explanation: The look your teacher gives you when they're trying to figure out if your dog really did eat your homework.

examples.text: Officials assessed the economy to see which areas needed more growth.
I assessed the pile of dishes in the sink and decided to go for a very long walk instead.

words.meaning: Goals that a person or group wants to reach.
To help something grow or become successful.
Happening in a very short time; very fast.
Times when work or activity is halted.

medium.simple_explanation: Occurrences where work or activity is halted or interrupted.
medium.funny_explanation: The real-world equivalent of your internet lagging just as you're about to win a game.

examples.text: Poor working conditions led to over 500 work stoppages in a single year.
There were several snack-related stoppages during our math study session.

words.meaning: Rooms or buildings used for living in.
Made longer or larger than usual.
Plans or preparations made for the future.

medium.simple_explanation: Plans or preparations made for a specific event or purpose.
medium.funny_explanation: The complicated web of lies and maneuvers required to get your siblings to do your chores for you.

examples.text: Special arrangements were made so that workers could attend university classes.
I made elaborate arrangements for my cat's birthday party, but she just wanted the cardboard box.

words.meaning: Places where small children are cared for during work.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The Soviet government set these up in factories so that women could work while their young children were cared for nearby.
hard.simple_explanation: A nursery or daycare center where babies and young children are cared for during the day.
hard.funny_explanation: A professional 'baby-parking' zone where toddlers hang out while their parents do serious adult work.

examples.text: The factory provided crèches to support working mothers.
The toddler escaped the crèche and was found trying to join the board meeting.

hard.real_world_analogy: A 'waiting room' filled with toys, nappies, and crying sounds instead of magazines and boring chairs.

words.meaning: Set up or started on a firm basis.

medium.simple_explanation: Set up on a firm or permanent basis.
medium.funny_explanation: Like when you 'establish' your territory on the couch by surrounding yourself with pillows and snacks.

examples.text: New health care centers were established in the factories for the workers.
I have established a new rule that says Monday mornings are officially canceled.

words.meaning: Useful materials or money available for use.
Kept within a certain size or amount.
A sign or object representing an idea.
Relating to the former government of Russia.

medium.simple_explanation: Referring to the former government of Russia and nearby countries (the USSR) where local councils held power.
medium.funny_explanation: Imagine a giant club where everyone has to share their snacks and the club president decides which games you play.

examples.text: The children studied the Soviet economy to understand how their country functioned.
The cat acted like a Soviet leader, demanding that all kibble in the house be distributed specifically to his bowl.

words.meaning: The system of trade and industry in a country.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The text mentions that Soviet children in the 1930s were specifically studying the Soviet economy.
hard.simple_explanation: The system by which a country's money, goods, and services are produced and used.
hard.funny_explanation: The complicated math of how many chocolates you can buy before your piggy bank starts crying.

examples.text: The government is trying to improve the national economy.
My personal economy is currently in a crisis because I spent all my pocket money on stickers.

hard.real_world_analogy: It's like a giant household budget for an entire country.

words.meaning: A place where goods are made by machines.
The act of eating a meal.
A place or thing where something comes from.

medium.simple_explanation: A place, person, or thing from which something comes or can be obtained, like a document used for evidence.
medium.funny_explanation: The original 'receipt' for a historical fact so people know you didn't just make it up in your dreams.

examples.text: The letter from the 13-year-old boy is a primary source for historians.
My dog is the primary source of the mysterious mud tracks across the living room carpet.

words.meaning: Hopes or thoughts about the future.
Things that are actually happening or true.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Used in the heading 'Dreams and Realities' to contrast the ideal Soviet childhood with the actual harsh life of the worker.
hard.simple_explanation: The state of things as they actually exist, rather than as they are imagined.
hard.funny_explanation: When you think you'll look like a movie star in the rain, but you actually look like a drowned rat.

examples.text: The realities of life in the mountains are very different from a holiday brochure.
The realities of having a cat involve more cleaning of hair than actual cuddling.

hard.real_world_analogy: Like looking at a photo without any filters or editing.

words.meaning: The period of time when a person is a child.
A person who does a job to earn money.

medium.simple_explanation: A person who performs labor or a specific job, often in a factory or manual setting.
medium.funny_explanation: The person who actually does the work while the boss practices their golf swing in the office.

examples.text: The young worker had to leave school to support his family at the factory.
The worker ant was annoyed because he had to carry a crumb three times his size while his friends were napping.

words.meaning: The official leader of a country or group.
A system where the community shares wealth and resources.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: It is the core political ideology discussed in the chapter title and the basis of the Soviet system.
hard.simple_explanation: A system where the community or government owns and controls resources so everyone can share them equally.
hard.funny_explanation: A system where if you bring a pack of chips to class, the teacher makes sure every single person gets exactly three chips.

examples.text: The leader promised to implement socialism to help the poor.
My brother only believes in socialism when it's time to share my birthday cake.

hard.real_world_analogy: A potluck dinner where everyone brings a dish, and everyone eats from every plate.

words.meaning: A total change in a country's government or system.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Refers to the Russian Revolution, which was the total overthrow of the old government.
hard.simple_explanation: A sudden, complete, and often violent change in the way a country is governed.
hard.funny_explanation: When the whole class decides to stop listening to the monitor and starts making their own rules.

examples.text: The industrial revolution changed the way people worked forever.
The students started a revolution when the canteen stopped serving samosas.

hard.real_world_analogy: Flipping a pancake; the side that was on the bottom is now suddenly on top.

words.meaning: A goal or principle that people support.

medium.simple_explanation: A principle, aim, or movement that, because of a deep belief, people support or fight for.
medium.funny_explanation: A fancy word for a 'reason' that usually involves wearing a cool t-shirt or carrying a sign.

examples.text: His father died fighting for the workers' cause to improve living conditions.
I am dedicated to the cause of making pizza a mandatory breakfast food.

words.meaning: Being sick or in poor health for a long time.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The young worker describes his mother as 'ailing', meaning she was too sick to work and support the family.
hard.simple_explanation: Experiencing illness or poor health, especially over a long period.
hard.funny_explanation: The sad state of a smartphone that only stays on for five minutes before dying.

examples.text: He stayed home to take care of his ailing grandmother.
My computer is ailing; it makes a sound like a vacuum cleaner whenever I open a game.

hard.real_world_analogy: A battery that won't hold a charge no matter how much you plug it in.

words.meaning: In a way that is total or whole.
To repair something that is broken or damaged.

medium.simple_explanation: To repair something that is broken, damaged, or torn.
medium.funny_explanation: What your grandmother does with a needle and thread, but what you try to do with an entire roll of duct tape.

examples.text: The boy's boots were so torn that no one could mend them anymore.
I tried to mend the vase I broke with glitter glue, but my mom wasn't fooled.

words.meaning: Coins or notes used to buy things.
A common food made from flour and water.
A specific job or piece of work to do.
People who are part of your family.
To stop something from happening.

medium.simple_explanation: To keep something from happening or arising.
medium.funny_explanation: The art of stopping a disaster before it starts, like catching a glass before it hits the floor.

examples.text: The boy went to work to prevent his family from falling into deeper poverty.
Wearing a helmet might prevent you from looking cool, but it also prevents your brain from becoming scrambled eggs.

words.meaning: Suffering or dying because of a lack of food.

medium.simple_explanation: Suffering or dying from hunger; needing food very badly.
medium.funny_explanation: What every teenager claims they are doing approximately twenty minutes after eating a full dinner.

examples.text: Without a job, the boy feared his family would end up starving.
I am literally starving, said the boy who had just eaten three apples and a bag of chips.

words.meaning: Official descriptions of a student's progress in school.
To print more copies of a book or text.

medium.simple_explanation: To print a new edition of a book or document that has already been published.
medium.funny_explanation: When a book is so popular (or important for school) that they have to hit the 'print' button on the big machine again.

examples.text: The textbook shows a reprint date of 2025-26 for this historical chapter.
I had to reprint my homework three times because my printer keeps eating the corners of the pages.

words.meaning: Organizing something into groups or collective units.

medium.simple_explanation: Turning many small, private farms into one giant, government-run farm where everyone works together.
medium.funny_explanation: Imagine your teacher forced the whole class to do one giant group project, and everyone had to share the same single grade regardless of who did the work.

examples.text: Stalin believed that collectivisation was the only way to modernize Soviet farming.
The cows were confused by collectivisation because they didn't know which farmer they were supposed to listen to anymore.

words.meaning: Very bad events that cause a lot of damage.
A very serious or severe problem.

medium.simple_explanation: A situation that is very serious, severe, or reaching a critical point quickly.
medium.funny_explanation: Think of it as a 'code red' situation, like realizing your homework is due in five minutes and you haven't started.

examples.text: The cities faced an acute shortage of bread during the winter months.
I have an acute need for a pizza right now or my stomach might actually stage a protest.

words.meaning: Amounts of things that are available to use.
Said no to something or would not do it.
Actions taken to achieve a particular result.
A supply of goods kept for future use.

medium.simple_explanation: A supply of goods or materials kept on hand for future use or sale.
medium.funny_explanation: Like that hidden pile of Halloween candy you keep under your bed for emergencies.

examples.text: The government believed that wealthy peasants were hiding grain stocks to sell them later at a higher price.
My stocks of clean socks have reached a dangerously low level this week.

words.meaning: Buying things hoping to sell them later for profit.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Describes the practice of traders holding back grain stocks to sell them later at higher prices during the food crisis.
hard.simple_explanation: The act of buying or holding something in the hope of making a large profit when its price increases in the future.
hard.funny_explanation: It's like refusing to eat your snacks now because you're betting that your friends will be so hungry later they'll trade you their whole lunch for one biscuit.

examples.text: The government took strict measures to stop speculation in the food market.
My brother's speculation that his rare sticker would be worth a fortune ended when he accidentally washed his pants with the sticker inside.

hard.real_world_analogy: Like a poker player holding onto their cards and waiting for the pot to get bigger before they reveal their hand.

words.meaning: Taken away by an authority figure.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Refers to the government's action of forcibly taking grain supplies from traders and 'kulaks'.
hard.simple_explanation: To have something taken away by an authority figure, usually as a punishment or to enforce a law.
hard.funny_explanation: That tragic moment when your teacher takes your comic book and puts it in the 'Drawer of No Return'.

examples.text: The customs officers confiscated the illegal items at the airport.
Mom confiscated the TV remote because we couldn't stop arguing over which cartoon to watch.

hard.real_world_analogy: Like a referee taking the ball away from a player who keeps breaking the rules.

words.meaning: Watching over an activity to ensure it is correct.

medium.simple_explanation: Watching over a task or a group of people to make sure everything is done correctly.
medium.funny_explanation: It's like being the 'hall monitor' of a farm, making sure nobody is slacking off behind a haystack.

examples.text: Party members spent the summer supervising the grain collection in the countryside.
Supervising my cat while she hunts a laser pointer is my favorite weekend activity.

words.meaning: Making sure that a rule or law is followed.

medium.simple_explanation: Compelling people to follow a rule, law, or command; making sure it happens by force if necessary.
medium.funny_explanation: When your mom says 'clean your room' and then stands in the doorway until you actually do it.

examples.text: The new laws for grain collection were strictly enforced by the local authorities.
The 'no-shoes-on-the-couch' rule is strictly enforced by my very grumpy bulldog.

words.meaning: Situations where there is not enough of something.
Updated to make something more current or advanced.

medium.simple_explanation: Bringing something up to date by using the latest technology or newer methods.
medium.funny_explanation: Trading in your ancient, brick-sized cell phone for the newest smartphone with 50 cameras.

examples.text: Stalin wanted to ensure that small peasant farms were modernised with tractors and machinery.
I modernised my homework routine by using a computer instead of a quill and ink.

words.meaning: To completely remove or get rid of something.

medium.simple_explanation: To completely get rid of or remove something or someone.
medium.funny_explanation: Like clicking the 'trash' icon on a computer file and then emptying the bin forever.

examples.text: The state aimed to eliminate the 'kulaks' to gain full control over the land.
I tried to eliminate all the vegetables from my plate, but my dad saw me feeding them to the dog.

words.meaning: To start or create something that will last.
Tools or equipment used for a specific task.

medium.simple_explanation: Tools or pieces of equipment used to perform a specific task, especially on a farm.
medium.funny_explanation: A fancy way of saying 'the stuff you use to do stuff,' like shovels, rakes, or even your favorite pen.

examples.text: Peasants had to give up their farming implements to the new collective farms.
The only implements I need for a successful weekend are a spoon and a giant tub of ice cream.

words.meaning: Moved from one place or person to another.
Very angry or furious about something.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Describes the extreme anger felt by peasants when they were forced to give up their land and livestock to collective farms.
hard.simple_explanation: Extremely angry or furious.
hard.funny_explanation: The level of anger you feel when you finally get to the front of the line and they tell you they just sold the last burger.

examples.text: The workers were enraged by the sudden decision to cut their wages.
The cat was enraged after we gave it a bath and spent the next hour knocking things off the table.

hard.real_world_analogy: Like a shaken-up soda bottle that is ready to explode the moment you touch the cap.

words.meaning: People who have the power to make decisions.

medium.simple_explanation: The people who have the power to make decisions, give orders, and enforce rules.
medium.funny_explanation: The 'big bosses'—basically anyone who can give you detention or a ticket.

examples.text: The peasants were afraid of the authorities who came to take their cattle.
The local authorities (my parents) have banned video games until I finish my chores.

words.meaning: Farm animals such as cows, sheep, and pigs.
In a very strict or harsh way.
Made to suffer for doing something wrong.
Forcibly removed from a country by law.

medium.simple_explanation: Being legally forced to leave a country, often as a punishment.
medium.funny_explanation: Getting kicked out of the party and told you can never come back to this house again.

examples.text: Many of those who resisted Stalin's plans were arrested and deported.
The spider was officially deported from my bedroom via a plastic cup and a piece of paper.

words.meaning: Forced to live away from one's own home country.

medium.simple_explanation: Being sent away from your home or country and forbidden to return, usually for political reasons.
medium.funny_explanation: Imagine being sent to your room, except your room is in a completely different country and you can't come out for years.

examples.text: Opponents of the regime were often exiled to remote parts of Siberia.
I felt like I was exiled to the 'kids' table' at the wedding while all the adults had the good cake.

words.meaning: Showing no pity or kindness toward others.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Describes how Stalin's government ignored the difficulties of independent farmers who didn't want to join collective farms.
hard.simple_explanation: Doing something in a way that shows no care, pity, or concern for someone else's feelings or problems.
hard.funny_explanation: It's like telling your friend 'that's nice' while they are crying because they dropped their ice cream.

examples.text: The judge looked unsympathetically at the thief's long list of excuses.
The alarm clock rings unsympathetically at 5 AM, totally ignoring how cozy my blanket is.

hard.real_world_analogy: Like a brick wall that doesn't care how hard you cry while leaning against it.

words.meaning: Causing a great amount of damage or destruction.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Describes the horrific famines in Soviet history that resulted in millions of deaths.
hard.simple_explanation: Causing great destruction, shock, or severe emotional pain.
hard.funny_explanation: The heartbreaking feeling when you realize your favorite white shirt has a permanent turmeric stain right in the middle.

examples.text: The flood had a devastating impact on the local crops.
It was a devastating blow to his reputation when he tripped over his own feet during the dance competition.

hard.real_world_analogy: Like a bowling ball crashing into a perfect set of pins, leaving nothing standing.

words.meaning: Extreme shortages of food leading to starvation.

The elves went on a striking mission because they wanted shorter hats and more cocoa.

words.meaning: An act of fighting against those in power.

medium.simple_explanation: An act where people fight back against a government or person in power.
medium.funny_explanation: The ultimate 'You're not the boss of me!' directed at a king or a queen.

examples.text: The worker was put on trial for his act of rebellion against the Tsar.
My cat started a rebellion by sitting on my keyboard until I fed him.

words.meaning: To write a first version of something.
Arguments used to prove someone is not guilty.

medium.simple_explanation: The speech or reasons someone gives to protect themselves from being blamed in court.
medium.funny_explanation: Your 'legal shield' used to explain why you aren't actually the person who broke the vase.

examples.text: Draft a speech to make in your defence before the judge.
My defence for being late was that a dragon blocked the driveway.

words.meaning: The title of a news story in a newspaper.
An act of resistance or a small rebellion.

medium.simple_explanation: A sudden and often violent act of a large group of people protesting against those in power.
medium.funny_explanation: Imagine the whole school suddenly standing on tables to demand free pizza—that's an uprising.

examples.text: The uprising of 24 October 1917 changed Russia forever.
There was a mini-uprising in the backyard when the squirrels decided they owned the birdfeeder.

words.meaning: Preferring traditional values and resisting quick change.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The text asks students to write a news item for a 'Conservative' paper regarding the 1917 uprising.
hard.simple_explanation: People or groups who prefer to keep things as they are and are cautious about changes or reforms.
hard.funny_explanation: The human equivalent of a 'Save' button that refuses to update the software because the old version worked just fine in 1995.

examples.text: The Conservative newspaper was horrified by the sudden overthrow of the traditional monarchy.
My conservative cat refuses to try new food and insists on the same cardboard-flavored kibble every morning.

hard.real_world_analogy: A person who refuses to switch from a physical map to GPS because they trust the old paper more.

words.meaning: Wanting deep and complete social or political change.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The activity requires writing a headline for a 'Radical' newspaper in Britain.
hard.simple_explanation: Supporting complete and extreme social or political change from the roots up.
hard.funny_explanation: The person who doesn't just want to clean the room, but wants to burn the house down and build a spaceship instead.

examples.text: Radical groups in Britain supported the idea of universal voting rights for all adults.
The radical student suggested replacing all school exams with a giant game of rock-paper-scissors.

hard.real_world_analogy: An IT guy who tells you to stop 'fixing' the computer and just format the whole hard drive.

words.meaning: A member of the Russian communist political party.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Bolsheviks were the major revolutionary group that eventually took control of Russia.
hard.simple_explanation: A member of the majority faction of the Russian Social Democratic Party that seized power in 1917.
hard.funny_explanation: The ultimate party-crashers who didn't just attend the party, they kicked the host out and renamed the house.

examples.text: The Bolsheviks, led by Lenin, gained support by promising 'Bread, Peace, and Land'.
If the Bolsheviks ran a school cafeteria, everyone would get exactly three peas and one potato, no matter how much they cried.

hard.real_world_analogy: A group of workers who decide the manager is useless and take over the company themselves.

words.meaning: A person who grows crops or keeps animals.
A system of combining small farms into large ones.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: It refers to Stalin's policy of forcing farmers to pool their land and resources.
hard.simple_explanation: A system where individual farms are combined into large, state-run farms.
hard.funny_explanation: Imagine being forced to share your personal lunchbox with the whole class, but the teacher gets to decide who eats the dessert.

examples.text: Stalin believed that collectivisation would solve the problem of grain shortages in Russia.
My siblings tried a policy of collectivisation with my Halloween candy, but somehow I ended up with only the wrappers.

hard.real_world_analogy: Converting several small family-owned shops into one giant government-run supermarket.

words.meaning: Feelings or expressions of disagreement or disapproval.

medium.simple_explanation: Statements or reasons showing that you disagree with a plan or idea.
medium.funny_explanation: The 'Wait just a minute!' points you make when your parents suggest more chores.

examples.text: The farmer wrote a letter to Stalin explaining his objections to the new laws.
I have several objections to the idea that broccoli is a dessert.

words.meaning: The state or situation in which people live.
An answer or a reaction to something.
Relating to society and how people live together.
Relating to money, trade, and industry of a country.

medium.simple_explanation: Relating to money, trade, and how a country manages its wealth.
medium.funny_explanation: A fancy word for everything involving cash, jobs, and why things cost so much.

examples.text: We need to study the economic conditions in Russia before the revolution.
My economic situation is looking bad because I spent all my allowance on stickers.

words.meaning: Relating to the government or public affairs.

medium.simple_explanation: Relating to the government, laws, and who holds power in a country.
medium.funny_explanation: Anything to do with the people who make the rules and wear the fancy suits.

examples.text: The political system in Russia was very strict under the Tsar.
The political debate in our house is about who gets to hold the TV remote.

words.meaning: All the people living in a particular area.
Relating to the system of rule by a Tsar.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The question asks why the 'Tsarist' autocracy collapsed in 1917.
hard.simple_explanation: Relating to the system of government ruled by a Tsar (the Emperor of Russia).
hard.funny_explanation: Anything belonging to the guy with the biggest crown and the most expensive fur coat in Russia.

examples.text: The Tsarist regime faced immense pressure during the First World War.
He walked around with such a Tsarist attitude that you'd think he owned the whole playground.

hard.real_world_analogy: An old-school principal who makes all the rules and never listens to the students.

words.meaning: A government where one person has absolute power.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The text discusses the collapse of the Russian autocracy.
hard.simple_explanation: A system of government where one person has absolute, unlimited power.
hard.funny_explanation: A 'one-man show' where the audience isn't allowed to leave or boo, and the star is also the judge.

examples.text: The people of Russia revolted against the autocracy to seek more democratic rights.
The toddler established an autocracy in the living room, declaring that only cartoons would be played forever.

hard.real_world_analogy: A remote control that only one person in the house is allowed to touch.

words.meaning: To fall down or fail suddenly and completely.

medium.simple_explanation: When a system or government fails completely and suddenly stops working.
medium.funny_explanation: Like a giant game of Jenga when someone pulls out the bottom block and everything goes 'CRASH'.

examples.text: Economic problems caused the Tsarist autocracy to collapse in 1917.
The tower of pancakes began to collapse as soon as I added the syrup.

words.meaning: Changes that happen as a result of an action.
The forceful overthrow of a government for a new system.

medium.simple_explanation: A total and radical change in the way a country is governed, usually by removing the old leaders.
medium.funny_explanation: A giant 'System Reset' button for a whole country.

examples.text: The October Revolution brought the Bolsheviks to power.
The students started a revolution to replace all pencils with glitter pens.

words.meaning: A strong effect or influence on someone or something.

medium.simple_explanation: The powerful effect that an event has on people or history.
medium.funny_explanation: The 'splash' left behind after a big event hits—like a cannonball in a swimming pool.

examples.text: The impact of the revolution was felt by everyone in Soviet history.
The impact of the flying pie was felt mostly by the clown's face.

words.meaning: Happening right away without any delay.
Wealthy peasants in Russia who owned land and labor.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The book asks for a description of 'kulaks' who were targeted during collectivisation.
hard.simple_explanation: Relatively wealthy peasants in late imperial Russia who owned larger farms and hired labor.
hard.funny_explanation: The village 'rich kids' who had a few extra sacks of grain and were treated like villains by the government.

examples.text: The kulaks were accused of hoarding grain and were severely punished by the state.
To the hungry villagers, the farmer with two tractors looked like a fancy kulak.

hard.real_world_analogy: A student who has a 64-pack of crayons while everyone else only has one broken pencil.

words.meaning: The elected legislative body or parliament in Russia.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The Duma was the elected parliament created by the Tsar after the 1905 Revolution.
hard.simple_explanation: A legislative body or parliament in Russia.
hard.funny_explanation: A talking shop that the Tsar opened when he was scared and closed whenever he got annoyed.

examples.text: The Tsar dismissed the first Duma within 75 days because he did not want his power questioned.
Our student council is like a Duma; we talk a lot, but the principal still makes all the real decisions.

hard.real_world_analogy: A suggestions box that looks fancy but is rarely actually opened by the boss.

words.meaning: People open to new ideas and individual freedoms.

medium.simple_explanation: People who believe in personal freedom and want the government to change things to make life fairer.
medium.funny_explanation: The people who think, 'Maybe we should actually ask folks what they want before we make a rule?'

examples.text: The Liberals in Russia wanted a government that respected individual rights.
The pizza liberals believe everyone has the right to choose their own crust thickness.

words.meaning: A plan of action or set of activities.
